title: Ten minutes of compassion
hook: put the compassion research into one sit

segments.voice: Yesterday was about caring for yourself as a carer. Your line was me too, because compassion includes the one doing the caring.

You can't sit with a finding on a Tuesday night. For a stretch of days, this path has piled them up. Feeling another's pain can swamp you; warmth and a wish to help hold up better. Carers wear out. The skill can be trained, it can widen to people unlike you, and it has to include the person doing it. Today the whole pile goes into one practice. An old one already exists for exactly this, with a set order of people and a short line to say to each.
screen: `A PILE OF FINDINGS.` → `ONE SIT TO HOLD THEM.` → `AN OLD ORDER, A SHORT LINE.`

segments.voice: First, the picture, back from the day on bias. The short discourse on loving-kindness in the Sutta Nipata aims at one image: a mother guarding her only child, held as a boundless heart toward every living being. The Pali word is metta, usually translated loving-kindness. Second, the order. A Theravada manual called the Path of Purification, which tradition credits to the commentator Buddhaghosa, lays out the whole route. Yesterday it supplied the starting point: yourself. Then someone dear. Then someone neutral, a face you pass without a thought. Then someone hostile. The aim, the manual says, is to break down the barriers between these people until the wish is the same for each. Third, what the research adds. The studies this path looked at suggest that feeling another's pain can drown you, while warmth and a wish to help hold up better. These phrases don't ask you to feel anyone's pain. They ask you to wish them well. And starting with yourself is yesterday's line, me too, built into the method. Fourth, when it sticks. Nothing has to be felt on cue. The manual expects resistance, especially at the hostile person, and advises going back to an easier person for a while, then returning. Teachers word the phrases differently; common ones are plain: may you be well, may you be safe, may you be at ease. And the ten minutes? Five stops, two minutes each.
screen: `THE MOTHER AND HER ONLY CHILD.` · `SELF, DEAR, NEUTRAL, HOSTILE.` · `WISH WELL, DON'T DROWN.` · `WHEN IT STICKS, GO BACK.` · then, large: `MAY YOU BE WELL.`

segments.voice: One quick pass through all five stops. Silently, to yourself first: may I be well, may I be safe, may I be at ease; then to someone dear; then a neutral face, a cashier or a neighbor whose name you never learned; then, only if it feels possible, someone difficult, and if not, stay a little longer with the neutral face; last, everyone at once. If you pray, you can hold these same people in your own prayer instead.
Ten minutes of compassion. Loving-kindness in the old manual's order: you, someone dear, someone neutral, someone hard, then everyone. Today's word.
Your line: may you be well. The full ten minutes is two for each of the five, whenever you have them. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In loving-kindness practice, Buddhists and others silently repeat short wishes such as "may you be well," moving from themselves to a dear person, a neutral person, a difficult person and finally all beings.

chat.says: Isn't compassion practice just trying to feel other people's pain?
options: No, it's wishing people well, in order: you, someone dear, a neutral face, someone hard, all.
Yes, the point is to take on their pain as your own until it swamps you.
Mostly, though you're meant to skip yourself and start with the hardest person.
chat.meaning: The phrases ask you to wish people well, not to feel their pain, moving from yourself to someone dear, neutral, hostile, then everyone.

notes: Confirm the paraphrase of the Karaniya Metta Sutta (Sn 1.8): as a mother would protect her only child with her life, so one should cultivate a boundless mind toward all beings.
Confirm the Visuddhimagga IX sequence (oneself, a dear person, a neutral person, a hostile person) and the aim of 'breaking down the barriers' (simasambheda) between them.
Confirm that Visuddhimagga IX advises returning to the earlier persons when resentment arises toward the hostile person, then returning to the hostile person.
The 'all beings' step at the end is the common modern teaching form; the Visuddhimagga's own extension to all beings comes after the barriers are broken down. Confirm wording.
The phrases 'may I be well / safe / at ease' are described as common modern wordings used by teachers, not a fixed traditional text.
The link to the empathy/compassion research recaps day 1304 (Singer and Klimecki) without new numbers.
